If Irwin’s adaptation of “The Imaginary Invalid,” directed by Brandon J. Dirden, is too stylized for many of the laughs to have landed for me, Moliere’s excoriating satire about doctors and the medical profession still resonates.

This revival of 'The Imaginary Invalid' has a bad case of anemia despite Brandon J. Dirden directing the Moliere classic as if it were a screwball comedy.
The romp and pageantry are delightful, and the show keeps audiences smiling and laughing the whole way through.
This 350-year-old text offers a blistering, laugh-out-loud critique of what happens when the fear of dying hollows out the joy of living.
In the end, The Imaginary Invalid makes a mountain of laughs out of a centuries-old Molière hill.
Funny costumes, funny wigs, and funny acting do not always add up to a funny farce when what's needed is a heart transplant.
Staging Invalid as a herky-jerky puppet show does not disguise the fact that we are watching a play about the fear of death.

cn.t: Bill Irwin's visually stunning revival of Molière's classic earns praise for its gorgeous design and timely healthcare satire, but critics are divided on whether the comedy lands—some find it hilarious, while others report muted laughter and overstylized performances.
